facts.fact: 'Janapada' comes from Jana (tribe) and Pada (feet): the land where a tribe settled.
Early Vedic clans were pastoral and moved in search of grazing land, so Janapada boundaries shifted.
The prime political objective of early Vedic clans was control of the best pasture lands.
In the Later Vedic Period (1000–600 BCE) the Jana took up agriculture and settled permanently in Janapadas.
Later Vedic states ('Rashtra') were either monarchical or republican.
From the 6th century BCE some Janapadas grew into larger Mahajanapadas.
Land replaced cattle as the most important source of wealth.
Iron weapons raised the political role of the warrior class.
New tools produced a surplus that the state could tax to support the army and administration.
Surplus production and trade led to the growth of towns and urban centres.
The term 'Mahajanapada' signifies the amalgamation of a large number of rural and urban settlements.
The age of the Mahajanapadas is dated c. 600–322 BCE (6th–4th century BCE).
There were sixteen Mahajanapadas in the Buddha’s time.
The Buddhist Anguttara Nikaya lists the sixteen Mahajanapadas.
The Buddhist Mahavastu also gives information on the Mahajanapadas.
The Jain Bhagavati Sutra gives a partly different list of sixteen Mahajanapadas.
Surasena (Shurasena), one of the sixteen in the Anguttara list, had its capital at Mathura.
Videha (Mithila) was one of the clans of the Vajji confederacy; the source text lists it in place of Surasena.
Magadha’s capital was Rajagriha (Bihar).
Kosala’s capital was Shravasti (Uttar Pradesh).
Vatsa’s capital was Kausambi (Uttar Pradesh).
Avanti’s capitals were Ujjaini (Ujjayini) and Mahishmati (Madhya Pradesh).
Gandhara’s capital was Taxila (present Pakistan/Afghanistan).
Kashi’s capital was Banaras (Varanasi).
Chedi’s capital was Suktimati (Madhya Pradesh).
Kuru’s capital was Hastinapur (Haryana/Delhi region).
Matsya’s capital was Virat Nagari (Viratnagar, Rajasthan).
Panchala’s capitals were Ahichhatra and Kampilya (Uttar Pradesh).
Anga’s capital was Champa (Bihar/Jharkhand).
Videha’s capital was Mithila (Bihar/Nepal).
Malla’s capitals were Kushinara and Pava.
Vajji’s capital was Vaishali (Bihar).
Kamboja’s capital was Rajpur (Rajapura).
Ashmaka’s capital was Potana (Potali).
Ashmaka (Assaka), on the Godavari, was the only Mahajanapada south of the Vindhyas.
Ashmaka’s capital Potana/Potali is usually identified with Bodhan (Nizamabad, Telangana); the source text places it in Maharashtra.
Assaka was separated from the neighbouring Mulaka by the Godavari.
Gandhara and Kamboja were the north-western Mahajanapadas.
Magadha’s economy rested on fertile Gangetic plains (rice) and trade in minerals and textiles.
Kosala grew wheat, barley and sugarcane and lay on major trade routes.
Vatsa (Kausambi) was a centre of culture and learning near the rivers.
Udayana was the famous king of Vatsa (Kausambi) in the Buddha’s time.
Ujjayini (Avanti) was a prominent trade and cultural centre.
Avanti was split by the Vindhyas: Ujjayini was the northern capital and Mahishmati the southern.
Avanti corresponds to the Malwa region of Madhya Pradesh.
Avanti’s Ujjayini lay on the Kshipra (Sipra), not the Mahanadi.
Gandhara lay on the Silk Road and was famed for Indo-Hellenistic fusion art.
Gandhara supplied men and material to the Achaemenid (Persian) army against the Greeks.
Taxila was the capital of Uttarapatha and a great centre of learning.
Pushkalavati, the other Gandhara capital, is modern Charsada (Pakistan).
Kashi was a centre of spirituality and learning with a rice economy.
Ancient Varanasi corresponds to the excavated site of Rajghat.
Chedi was known for valorous warriors.
Kuru (Hastinapur) is associated with the Mahabharata.
Matsya took its name from aquatic life (matsya = fish).
Panchala was associated with Vedic rituals and scholarship.
Kampilya (Panchala) is modern Kampil in Uttar Pradesh.
Anga (Champa) is credited with the invention of the veena.
Videha (Mithila) is associated with the sage Yajnavalkya.
The Buddha attained Mahaparinirvana at Kushinara in Malla territory.
Kamboja was famous for horse-rearing and the horse trade.
Kamboja–Vipas (Beas) is a wrong region–river pair (UPSC 2025).
Kosala lay on the Sarayu river.
Shravasti (Kosala) is the modern site of Sahet–Mahet.
Kosala and Magadha are the kingdoms most associated with the Buddha’s life.
In the monarchies power was generally hereditary and the king held supreme, centralised authority.
Monarchies had a well-defined class structure and rigid hierarchies.
Republics were governed by collective decision-making rather than a single monarch.
Republics were called 'Ganas' or 'Sanghas'.
Gana-sanghas were governed by a council of representatives of the ruling clans — oligarchies.
In the gana-sanghas the king (chief) was elected and ruled with a council.
The governing assembly of a republic was the Ganaparishad.
Gana-sangha assemblies met in a hall called the santhagara.
Magadha, Kosala, Avanti and Vatsa were monarchies, not republics.
The source text names Assaka, Malla and Vajji as the republican Mahajanapadas.
Vajji (Vriji) was the most powerful Mahajanapada governed under the Sangha (gana) system.
Vajji was a confederacy of eight clans, of which the Licchavis were the most important.
The Shakyas of Kapilavastu and the Koliyas were other gana-sanghas (republics).
The founders of Jainism and Buddhism came from republican states.
Mahavira was born at Kundagrama near Vaishali in the Vajji republic; the Buddha was a Shakya.
The source text also lists Kuru, Panchala and Kamboja as assembly-governed republics, contradicting its own monarchy list.
Jainism and Buddhism challenged the orthodoxy of Vedic religion and advocated a simpler, ethical life.
Both Jainism and Buddhism promoted Ahimsa (non-violence).
The growth of towns in this age is called the 'second urbanisation' (after the Harappan cities).
Punch-marked coins emerged, marking the beginning of a formalised monetary economy.
Pali texts name coins such as kahapana (karshapana), nikkha, kamsa and kakanika — evidence of urban life and a money economy.
Punch-marked coins were mostly silver (some copper) and bore symbols, not inscriptions.
Urbanisation fostered trade and the rise of merchant and artisan communities.
Northern Black Polished Ware (NBPW) was the prominent pottery of the Mahajanapada period.
Large-scale use of iron tools allowed forest clearing and the expansion of agriculture.
Merchants and artisans were organised into guilds called sartha.
Iron tools such as axes, adzes and sickles helped agriculture flourish.
Crops included paddy, barley, cotton, pulses and sugarcane.
Farmers paid one-sixth (1/6) of their produce as land tax, called 'Bhaga'.
Merchants and peasants were also taxed through 'Bali'.
Rich merchants/landowners were called grihapatis.
Craftsmen, herders, hunters and traders were all subject to taxes.
Iron ploughshares came into wider use and raised output.
Paddy was transplanted from saplings instead of broadcasting seed, raising yield but also labour.
Social stratification grew, with distinct classes of merchants, settlers and peasants.
The position of women declined except within the Buddhist and Jain orders.
The caste system became more rigid and untouchability worsened.
Multi-caste villages were headed by a Bhojaka.
A second type of village — suburban — was dominated by craftsmen.
Villages on the outskirts were inhabited by fowlers and hunters.
Writing came into common use for bookkeeping, taxation and army administration.
The king, primarily a warlord, was the highest administrative official.
Ministers were called Mahamatras.
Army commanders were called Senanayaka.
Villages were run by a headman, the Gramabhojaka or Gramini, who also collected taxes.
The new Rajas maintained regular (standing) armies.
Most capitals were fortified for security against rival rulers.
Each Mahajanapada had its own capital.
Magadha emerged as the most powerful of the sixteen under Bimbisara.
Magadha became the nerve centre of political activity in North India.
The Magadha Empire was the first empire in India.
